section_summary: This section documents U.S. monitoring and control of strategic-material exports to Japan, including mercury, molybdenite, scrap iron, cotton, petroleum products, zinc, lead, chrome ore, and North African minerals. It combines diplomatic and intelligence reporting from Latin America, Haiti, Morocco, and Japan with congressional and public correspondence advocating tighter embargoes. Several files concern Japanese purchasing agent Koichiro Kuzutani, Dominican and Haitian scrap-iron policy, and German-Japanese efforts to obtain Moroccan manganese, cobalt, and molybdenum.

subfiles.title: Mercury shipments from Manzanillo
subfiles.from: Henry A. Hoyt, American Vice Consul, Manzanillo
subfiles.about: Reports mercury shipments from Manzanillo to Japan since January 1, 1941.
subfiles.summary: Hoyt lists six Japanese vessels carrying a total of 5,156 flasks of mercury between January 23 and March 7. Local agents valued each seventy-five-pound flask at approximately $192 and expected further shipments.

subfiles.title: Molybdenite shipment from Colombia to Japan
subfiles.about: Reports a Colombian shipment of molybdenite concentrates destined for Japan.
subfiles.summary: British consular information indicated that twenty-two tons of molybdenite concentrates left Colombia on the Japanese vessel Guayo Maru, which reached Los Angeles on December 22, 1940. The embassy believed this was Colombia's first and only such shipment to Japan.

subfiles.title: Transmittal of memoranda on Latin American exports
subfiles.from: Herbert Feis, for the Secretary of State
subfiles.about: Forwards additional memoranda concerning exports from Central and South America.
subfiles.summary: Feis sends copies of further memoranda on exports from Central and South America to Japan, Germany, and Russia. The page functions as a short covering letter for the enclosed economic material.

subfiles.title: FBI transmittal to Assistant Secretary Berle
subfiles.about: Transmits FBI data believed potentially useful to the State Department.
subfiles.summary: Hoover forwards unspecified information to Assistant Secretary Berle for his attention. The following FBI report appears to be the enclosed material.

subfiles.title: FBI report on Lufkin Rule Company export policy
subfiles.from: N. C. Eberstein, FBI special agent
subfiles.about: Records the Lufkin Rule Company's policy against sales of precision instruments to Japan or Russia.
subfiles.summary: Company president A. G. Thompson stated that since September 1939 his firm had refused sales to Japan and Russia because its instruments were important to national defense. He said the company investigated suspicious orders and warned that large orders specifying metric measurements might indicate an ultimate Japanese or Russian destination.

subfiles.title: Senator Barbour's transmittal of Helen Wright's inquiry
subfiles.about: Forwards Helen C. Wright's questions about restrictions on exports to Japan.
subfiles.summary: Senator Barbour asks the Department to communicate directly with Wright and supply the information she requests. Her enclosed letter concerns the legal and practical extent of the supposed embargo against Japan.

subfiles.title: Helen C. Wright's questions about the Japanese embargo
subfiles.about: Requests detailed information about laws and enforcement restricting raw-material exports to Japan.
subfiles.summary: Wright asks whether Congress enacted an embargo, when it began, what products it covers, how effective it is, and which agency enforces it. She explains that a radio forum left her uncertain whether any embargo existed and also asks for a Senate gallery ticket.

subfiles.title: State Department reply to Senator Barbour
subfiles.about: Acknowledges Wright's inquiry and encloses the Department's direct response.
subfiles.summary: The Department acknowledges Barbour's March 20 letter concerning export restrictions on Japan. It informs him that a copy of the detailed reply being sent to Wright is enclosed.

subfiles.title: State Department explanation of export-control law to Helen Wright
subfiles.from: Leonard H. Price, for the Secretary of State
subfiles.about: Explains the statutory basis, product coverage, and administration of U.S. export controls.
subfiles.summary: Price states that Congress had enacted no embargo applying exclusively to one country, but Section 6 of the July 2, 1940 act authorized the President to control exports for national defense. He describes licensing requirements covering metals, hides, rubber, fibers, machinery, chemicals, and aviation fuels and explains the respective roles of the State Department and Administrator of Export Control. Wright is directed to the Commerce Department for current trade statistics.

subfiles.title: Sale of Haitian cotton to Japan
subfiles.about: Reports British information and Haitian economic considerations surrounding a prospective cotton sale to Japan.
subfiles.summary: White's British colleague believed the cotton would probably be made into gun cotton rather than sent through Siberia to Germany. He warned that a successful transaction could lead to another thirteen to fifteen thousand bales being sold to Japan. White stressed Haiti's urgent need to dispose of its cotton and requested the Department's views.

subfiles.title: Reply concerning Haitian cotton outlets
subfiles.about: Responds to White's reports on sales of Haitian cotton to Japanese interests.
subfiles.summary: The Department says it has fewer means to suggest alternative outlets for Haitian cotton than for controlled goods such as scrap iron. It notes that the United States cannot restrict exports from Haiti and again suggests approaching British purchasing agents in the United States.

subfiles.title: Mrs. Schober's protest against Philippine exports to Japan
subfiles.about: Urges stronger federal action against Japanese access to materials from the Philippines.
subfiles.summary: Schober cites a letter from Woodbury Willoughby stating that the President's executive order did not prohibit certain Philippine shipments to Japan. She describes Japanese influence in the islands as alarming and asks the government to find a remedy.

subfiles.title: Senator Sheppard's transmittal of Mrs. Campbell's letter
subfiles.about: Forwards a constituent's demand for an embargo on materials sent to Japan.
subfiles.summary: Sheppard encloses Mrs. L. P. Campbell's letter from Lufkin, Texas. He asks the Secretary for a statement of the current situation that he can use in answering her.

subfiles.title: Lufkin churchwomen's appeal for an embargo
subfiles.about: Calls for an embargo on oil, gasoline, cotton, and other war materials going to Japan.
subfiles.summary: Campbell writes on behalf of women from Protestant churches studying China. She argues that halting war-material exports to Japan and other aggressor states would help China more than charitable donations and appeals to Christian and patriotic principles.

subfiles.title: State Department reply to Senator Sheppard
subfiles.about: Explains existing export controls in response to Mrs. Campbell's embargo appeal.
subfiles.summary: The Department emphasizes that no statute singles out one country, but presidential proclamations under the July 2, 1940 act require licenses for many strategic commodities. Controlled items include metals, petroleum products, chemicals, cotton linters, wool, machinery, arms, and munitions. It assures Campbell that national-defense considerations govern every license decision.

subfiles.title: Market for Dominican scrap iron
subfiles.about: Records Dominican cooperation in blocking scrap-iron exports to Japan and a request for American buyers.
subfiles.summary: Minister Pastoriza said President Troncoso had stopped a shipment scheduled for Japan after informing Minister Scotten of Dominican policy. Pastoriza requested names of prospective American purchasers, and Barber supplied seven firms while disclaiming departmental responsibility for them.

subfiles.title: Instruction transmitting scrap-iron buyer contacts
subfiles.about: Transmits the March 3 conversation memorandum and authorizes sharing prospective buyers with Dominican officials.
subfiles.summary: The instruction refers to earlier discussions of Dominican scrap-iron sales and sends a copy of Barber's memorandum. The legation may give the listed business contacts to Dominican authorities, provided it states that neither the Department nor the legation assumes responsibility for them.

subfiles.title: Enclosed copy of memorandum on Dominican scrap iron
subfiles.about: Duplicates the memorandum describing Dominican efforts to prevent a scrap shipment to Japan.
subfiles.summary: The copy repeats Pastoriza's account that President Troncoso had stopped the proposed March 6 shipment. It also reproduces the names and addresses of seven prospective American scrap-iron purchasers.

subfiles.title: Report of a Haitian-Mitsui scrap-iron agreement
subfiles.about: Reports Dominican information that Haiti had agreed to permit scrap-iron exports to Japan through Mitsui.
subfiles.summary: The Dominican foreign minister relayed a report from his legation in Port-au-Prince that the Haitian government and Mitsui had reached an agreement. Scotten inferred that the Dominican government would resent Haitian exports after agreeing to block comparable Dominican shipments.

subfiles.title: Japanese cotton buyer reported in Managua
subfiles.about: Relays Panama Canal intelligence about a Japanese agent seeking Nicaraguan cotton.
subfiles.summary: Canal intelligence reported that a Japanese government purchasing agent was in Managua attempting to buy cotton for shipment to Japan via Balboa. The continuation is badly garbled, but it concerns the buyer's activities and prospective shipment arrangements.

subfiles.title: European Affairs memorandum on cotton exports to the Soviet Union
subfiles.about: Suggests language for answering concerns that American cotton sent to the Soviet Union might indirectly benefit Germany.
subfiles.summary: The memorandum gives 1940 exports as approximately 139,000 bales valued at $7.864 million. It concedes that American cotton might replace Soviet cotton shipped to Germany but says the Department has no evidence, citing the Soviet ambassador's assurance that U.S. purchases were solely for domestic needs.

subfiles.title: Houston committee inquiry on gasoline and Soviet cotton
subfiles.about: Asks about ordinary gasoline exports to Japan and cotton shipments to the Soviet Union.
subfiles.summary: Bradley notes claims that ordinary gasoline could be converted into aviation fuel and urges consideration of stopping all gasoline shipments to Japan. He also asks whether American cotton reaching Vladivostok was replacing Soviet goods transferred to Germany.

subfiles.title: Reply to the Houston Committee to Defend America
subfiles.about: Answers questions about gasoline conversion and cotton exports to the Soviet Union.
subfiles.summary: Price says aviation-gasoline regulations account for the possibility of raising octane through tetraethyl lead. He supplies the 1940 cotton-export figures but says there is no official evidence that American cotton enabled Soviet cotton to reach Germany. A press release containing the Soviet ambassador's assurance of domestic use is enclosed; the file includes a repeated or alternate first-page copy.

subfiles.title: Philippine Affairs wording on export-control jurisdiction
subfiles.about: Corrects proposed wording about the Philippines' constitutional position and export-control status.
subfiles.summary: Richards warns that saying the Philippines was outside U.S. sovereignty would be misleading. He proposes explaining that controls apply to exports from the United States, its territories, and possessions except the Philippine Islands; shipments to the islands are controlled, but exports from them are not.

subfiles.title: Senator Burton inquiry on Philippine exports
subfiles.about: Requests information about iron ore and vegetable oils reportedly shipped from the Philippines to Japan and Russia.
subfiles.summary: Burton forwards concerns from Sheldon F. Echfeld that Philippine materials sent to Japan or Russia might ultimately reach Germany. He asks for the government's policy regarding shipments from the United States and its possessions.

subfiles.title: Secretary Hull's reply on Philippine and vegetable-oil exports
subfiles.about: Explains the Philippine exception to U.S. export controls and new licensing of vegetable oils.
subfiles.summary: Hull states that Section 6 restrictions apply throughout U.S. territory except to exports originating in the Philippine Islands, although shipments from the United States to the islands remain controlled. He adds that important iron ores and certain vegetable oils already require licenses for Japan and Russia and that, effective April 15, controls will cover all vegetable oils, fats, and oil-bearing raw materials.

subfiles.title: President Troncoso reaffirms Dominican scrap-iron prohibition
subfiles.about: Reports categorical Dominican assurances that no scrap iron will be exported to Japan.
subfiles.summary: Troncoso showed Scotten orders denying Soto Mayor's request to export scrap to Japan. He repeated reports of a Haitian-Japanese arrangement allegedly involving Senator Norl and President Vincent and pledged Dominican cooperation with the United States on hemisphere defense.

subfiles.title: Instruction to investigate Haitian scrap-iron agreement
subfiles.about: Orders an urgent inquiry into reports of a Haitian agreement with Mitsui for scrap-iron exports.
subfiles.summary: The Department directs the legation to investigate without disclosing the Dominican source. It asks the minister to cite export-control measures adopted by Colombia, Cuba, Mexico, and other countries and confidentially express the hope that Haiti will follow the same defense policy.

subfiles.title: Haitian denial and request for scrap-iron buyers
subfiles.about: Reports Haiti's denial of an official Mitsui agreement and requests names of prospective purchasers.
subfiles.summary: The Haitian foreign minister denied any official arrangement, although Mitsui's representative was reportedly seeking both scrap iron and cotton. White estimated that 2,500–3,000 tons of scrap were available and said export control would be easier if American or British buyers could take the material.

subfiles.title: Instruction forwarding Cuba export-control press release
subfiles.about: Sends Cuba's export-control press release in response to the Haitian scrap-iron inquiry.
subfiles.summary: The Department transmits two copies of Press Release No. 130 of March 26. The release concerns Cuban reexport prohibitions and new general U.S. export licenses for controlled materials sent to Cuba.

subfiles.title: General export licenses for Cuba
subfiles.about: Announces general licenses for specified controlled materials exported to Cuba.
subfiles.summary: Because Cuba had imposed reexport prohibitions, the State Department issued general licenses covering antimony, asbestos, chromium, hides, molybdenum, quartz crystals, rubber, silk, chemicals, wool, and numerous iron and steel forms. Exporters still had to cite the appropriate license, while controlled products omitted from the list continued to require individual licenses. Similar arrangements with other Western Hemisphere countries were contemplated.

subfiles.title: Senate referral of Lydia Walkup's letter
subfiles.about: Refers a constituent's complaint about scrap-iron sales to Japan for departmental comment.
subfiles.summary: The Senate office sends the enclosed communication to Hull for favorable consideration and a report. It requests that the enclosure be returned with the Department's response.

subfiles.title: Lydia Walkup's demand for a strict Japanese embargo
subfiles.about: Questions reported Japanese purchases of lower-grade scrap and urges a comprehensive embargo.
subfiles.summary: Walkup says she believed the scrap-iron embargo barred sales to Japan but heard that Japan was still purchasing Class B and C scrap. Citing sympathy for China and Japanese hostility toward the United States, she asks Lee to support a strict embargo on all munitions and warlike materials.

subfiles.title: Secretary Hull's reply to Senator Lee
subfiles.about: Explains that all grades of iron and steel scrap were already barred from shipment to Japan.
subfiles.summary: Hull says the July 1940 proclamation initially covered only some scrap grades, but the October 16 extension brought all iron and steel scrap under control. Licenses were being granted only for Western Hemisphere countries and Great Britain. He also lists other controlled raw materials, manufactures, petroleum, and aviation products.

subfiles.title: Conversation on the Japan Gasolene–Universal Oil settlement
subfiles.about: Records Morishima's request for expedited approval of a corporate settlement.
subfiles.summary: Morishima said the Japan Gasolene Company and Universal Oil Company had virtually agreed on settlement terms except for moral-embargo items. He asked Berle to expedite the Department's response and suggested he might execute the papers himself instead of requiring the Japanese company's president to travel to the United States.

subfiles.title: FBI circulation or transmittal sheet
subfiles.to: Department of State; copies to Alan Goodrich Kirk and Sherman Miles
subfiles.about: Circulates an incompletely legible intelligence communication among State, Navy, and War officials.
subfiles.summary: The surviving page is largely obscured but bears FBI letterhead and State Department routing marks. It identifies the naval and military intelligence chiefs as copy recipients, indicating interdepartmental circulation of security information.

subfiles.title: Japanese purchasing agent in Managua
subfiles.about: Summarizes information about Koichiro Kuzutani's purchase of Nicaraguan cotton.
subfiles.summary: The memorandum reports that the cotton transaction had apparently been completed and was probably connected with munitions or powder production. United Fruit was uncertain whether to carry the cotton to the Canal Zone because the United States might block transshipment. The agent was identified as Koichiro Kuzutani, also recently reported from Haiti.

subfiles.title: Visa inquiry concerning Koichiro Kuzutani
subfiles.about: Requests guidance on whether Japanese commercial agent Koichiro Kuzutani qualifies as a bona fide temporary visitor.
subfiles.summary: White reports that Kuzutani, an Osaka-born Japanese national, sought a U.S. nonimmigrant visa after traveling through Nicaragua and El Salvador. He was associated with Mitsui or Mitsui Bussan Kaisha and intended to continue as manager of the New York branch of a Dallas cotton company. White asks whether he should be regarded as a genuine temporary visitor.

subfiles.title: Instruction to investigate Kuzutani in Nicaragua
subfiles.about: Requests information about Koichiro Kuzutani's activities in Nicaragua.
subfiles.summary: The Department summarizes Kuzutani's affiliations, U.S. visa application, and recent travel through Nicaragua and El Salvador. It asks the Managua legation to report by air mail before a decision is made on his visa.

subfiles.title: Interim instruction on Kuzutani's visa application
subfiles.about: Acknowledges Kuzutani's visa case and postpones a decision pending regional investigations.
subfiles.summary: The Department says the legations in Managua and San Salvador have been asked to investigate Kuzutani's activities. White is instructed to send any additional information about his conduct in Haiti while awaiting further guidance.

subfiles.title: Instruction to investigate Kuzutani in El Salvador
subfiles.about: Requests information about Koichiro Kuzutani's activities in El Salvador.
subfiles.summary: The Department repeats the account of Kuzutani's commercial affiliations and requested U.S. visit. It asks the San Salvador legation for an air-mail report on his activities during his recent trip through El Salvador.

subfiles.title: Memorandum on Japanese cotton purchases and Esteban Prieto
subfiles.to: Mr. Finley, Mr. Hooker, and Mr. Collado
subfiles.about: Summarizes reports on Kuzutani's Haitian cotton plans and Mitsui representative Esteban Prieto.
subfiles.summary: White's British colleague reported that Kuzutani was prepared to buy substantial cotton and arrange transport through his firm's own steamers. The memorandum also notes a thousand-bale sale to Colombia and American interest in cotton formerly supplied from India. It recalls allegations that former Japanese consul Esteban Prieto offered campaign contributions for favorable treatment of Japanese commercial ventures.

subfiles.title: Further report on Kuzutani and Haitian cotton
subfiles.about: Reports Kuzutani's willingness to buy Haitian cotton and arrange shipment through Mitsui vessels.
subfiles.summary: The British minister said Kuzutani was ready to purchase a substantial amount of cotton and arrange transshipment through his firm's fleet. Haitian commercial authorities professed no knowledge of Japanese buying, though a thousand-bale contract with Colombia and an inquiry from South Carolina were reported. The despatch links the buyer to Mitsui and to the pending U.S. visa inquiry.

subfiles.title: Senator Burton inquiry concerning zinc exports
subfiles.about: Forwards an Ohio manufacturer's concern that zinc exports to Japan were causing domestic scarcity.
subfiles.summary: Burton encloses excerpts from Charles T. Austin of the Ohio Bronze Powder Company. He asks for the government's present zinc-export policy and whether any change is under consideration.

subfiles.title: Charles Austin's statement on zinc shortages
subfiles.about: Describes a critical shortage of ingot zinc needed to manufacture bronze powders.
subfiles.summary: Austin says the Ohio Bronze Powder Company increasingly cannot obtain zinc flabs or ingots and may have to stop production. He attributes at least part of the shortage to exports to Japan and other antagonistic countries and asks for government relief.

subfiles.title: Secretary Hull's reply on zinc controls
subfiles.about: States that zinc exports to Japan had been denied after zinc came under license control.
subfiles.summary: Hull explains that the January 10 presidential proclamation placed zinc under export control effective February 3. Because zinc was urgently needed for national defense, applications to export it to Japan had been disapproved.

subfiles.title: Japanese efforts to acquire lead
subfiles.from: Office of the Adviser on International Economic Affairs
subfiles.about: Calls attention to a report that Japanese interests were seeking several thousand tons of lead.
subfiles.summary: The memorandum quotes a Wall Street Journal item describing Japanese inquiries for lead, possibly of foreign origin because of the high asking price. It notes that, unlike copper and zinc, lead did not then require an export license.

subfiles.title: Mexican lead shipments to Japan
subfiles.about: Provides statistics on in-transit Mexican lead shipments to Japan during five months of 1940.
subfiles.summary: Barton lists monthly poundage and value for January, February, October, November, and December. The recorded shipments total large quantities of Mexican lead moving in transit to Japan, while no corresponding shipments to Russia were found for the specified period.

subfiles.title: Acknowledgment of lead-shipment statistics
subfiles.about: Thanks the Commerce Department for compiling Mexican lead-shipment data.
subfiles.summary: Stinebower acknowledges Barton's March 10 statistics on in-transit lead shipments from Mexico to Japan. He notes that the compilation required substantial work and expresses the Department's appreciation.

subfiles.title: Japanese and German interests in Moroccan minerals
subfiles.about: Reports extensive Japanese and German efforts to obtain Moroccan manganese, cobalt, and molybdenum.
subfiles.summary: A Japanese government mission was negotiating with German armistice officials, Mitsui, Jean Epinat, and Moroccan mining companies for minerals needed by Japanese war industries. Stanton describes the mines, ownership, ore grades, stocks, Japanese orders, proposed tea-and-textile offsets, and severe land and ocean transportation problems. He reports German pressure for expanded production and shipments to France and Germany, while noting that the French Moroccan Residency appeared to obstruct the pro-German Omnium group's transport access.

subfiles.title: Feis letter on possible U.S. purchases of Moroccan minerals
subfiles.about: Forwards the Casablanca mineral report and asks whether U.S. procurement should be reconsidered.
subfiles.summary: Feis sends Stanton's confidential despatch on German and Japanese efforts to obtain Moroccan manganese, cobalt, and molybdenum. He recalls that earlier U.S. purchasing proposals were discouraged by the Army and Navy Munitions Board and invites Henderson to consider whether the Office of Production Management or Federal Loan Administrator should now act.

subfiles.title: FBI transmittal of intelligence on Japanese industry
subfiles.about: Transmits a photostatic memorandum describing industrial conditions in Japan.
subfiles.summary: Hoover forwards recent information on Japanese industrial conditions for Berle's possible interest. Copies were also directed to the heads of naval and army intelligence.

subfiles.title: Japan: Industrial
subfiles.to: Adolf A. Berle Jr. and intelligence agencies
subfiles.about: Lists Japanese armaments production, construction, imports, and shortages.
subfiles.summary: The memorandum identifies government work at Tennōji, armor and gun production at Hirakata Arsenal, and major new munitions facilities near Sakai and Nishinomiya. It also reports annual asbestos imports from Africa valued at seven million dollars and shortages of shoe leather, matches, and rubber.

subfiles.title: Further conversation on the Universal Oil settlement
subfiles.about: Records Morishima's renewed request to complete the Universal Oil Company settlement.
subfiles.summary: Morishima asked whether the settlement arrangements were proceeding and expressed a desire to resolve them before leaving for New York. Berle replied that he knew of no difficulty and would do what he could to advance the matter.

subfiles.title: Acknowledgment of British information on Japanese chrome-ore inquiries
subfiles.about: Thanks the British Embassy for information about Japanese inquiries for chrome ore.
subfiles.summary: Davis acknowledges Thorold's March 26 note reporting Japanese interest in chrome ore packed in sacks for delivery to Japanese ports, Vladivostok, or Dairen. He states that the Department welcomes information of this kind. Page 215 is a duplicate OCR copy of the same letter.
